extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in religion, Christian apologetics, and philosophical reflection
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt of a philosophical/theological essay (Pensées) discussing how belief is formed and defended, the roles of reason, custom, and inspiration, and reflections on justice and social authority. It offers practical and epistemic criteria for cultivating and evaluating faith and social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act as if you believed
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the way by which others began; by acting as if you believed, taking the holy water, having masses said, etc. Even this will naturally make you believe, and deaden your acuteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical participation (externals) will lessen passions and eventually produce faith; you will become faithful, honest, humble, grateful, generous, a sincere friend, truthful. You gain in this life and risk little — it is a prudent wager for something certain and infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for the truth (seek signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the doctrine of chance, you ought to put yourself to the trouble of searching for the truth; if you die without worshipping the True Cause, you are lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: God has left signs of His will; one must seek them rather than neglect them — it is well worth the effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three sources of belief: reason, custom, inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three sources of belief: reason, custom, inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Christian religion acknowledges all three but holds that true, saving faith is ultimately a gift of inspiration; reason must be opened to proofs, and belief should be confirmed by custom and humility toward inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Join externals to internals (avoid superstition and pride)
rubrics_metrics.description: The external must be joined to the internal to obtain anything from God: we must kneel, pray with the lips, etc.; to expect help from these externals alone is superstition; to refuse them is pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use outward practices to incline the will; do not rely solely on formalities (superstition) nor refuse them (pride). Both inward disposition and outward observance are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom as the primary practical source of strong belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom is the source of our strongest and most believed proofs; it bends the automaton, which persuades the mind without its thinking about the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reason is fallible and intermittent, one should secure faith by habit/custom so belief does not vacillate; use custom to keep the automaton from inclining to the contrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith is a gift; proofs are instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith is different from proof; the one is human, the other is a gift of God. Proof is often the instrument; fides ex auditu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While reasoning and proofs can prepare and assist, saving faith itself is given by God; proofs convert by preparing the heart but do not replace divine inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes about reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Two extremes: to exclude reason, to admit reason only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither absolute exclusion of reason nor its sole admission is correct; a balanced use of reason in combination with other sources is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know where to doubt, where to feel certain, where to submit
rubrics_metrics.description: We must know where to doubt, where to feel certain, where to submit. He who does not do so understands not the force of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission (yielding) is itself a use of reason and consists in true Christianity; reason should judge when submission is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heart intuition of first principles
rubrics_metrics.description: We know truth not only by reason but also by the heart; the heart intuits first principles (space, time, motion, number) which reason cannot prove but must trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason should be humbled by its inability to supply these intuitions; skeptics who demand reason's proofs for these intuitions misunderstand the sources of human knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the order of the heart when persuading the faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: The heart has its own order; it does not prove by enumeration but warms and inclines through digressions that keep the end in sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing souls who require warmth more than instruction, employ the heart's order (appeal to love, digressions toward the end) rather than purely intellectual demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility of heart and learning are both valid paths to belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds know God: those with a humble heart inclined to love and those with sufficient understanding to see the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple believers who feel an inward disposition may be genuinely inspired; learned believers can trace proofs. Both forms may yield true faith, though their evidence differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs of religion — enumerated evidences
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of proofs for religion: (1) The establishment of the Christian religion, (2) the sanctity/dignity/humility of the Christian soul, (3) the miracles of Holy Scripture, (4) Jesus Christ, (5) the apostles, (6) Moses and the prophets, (7) the Jewish people, (8) the prophecies, (9) perpetuity (no religion has perpetuity), (10) the doctrine which gives a reason for everything, (11) the sanctity of the law, (12) the course of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items together constitute the cumulative case for the Christian religion; elsewhere condensed as Morality, Doctrine, Miracles, Prophecies, Types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish piety from superstition
rubrics_metrics.description: Piety is different from superstition; to carry piety as far as superstition is to destroy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of superstitious submission (doing things solely as formalities) and of rejecting true piety because it includes external signs not perceived by reason alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief should be personal assent, not mere appeal to authority
rubrics_metrics.description: So far from making it a rule to believe a thing because you have heard it, you ought to believe nothing without putting yourself in the position as if you had never heard it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your own assent and the constant voice of your reason should make you believe; do not rely solely on antiquity, general consent, or authority as the rule of belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of reason (Augustine’s point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason would never submit if it did not judge that there are some occasions on which it ought to submit; it is then right for it to submit when it judges that it ought to submit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission is not the negation of reason but its proper exercise in certain domains where reason recognizes its limits and elects to yield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom creates justice (custom as source of law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom creates the whole of equity; nothing is so faulty as those laws which correct faults. There are natural laws, but custom and human caprice often determine justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because human laws and opinions vary by place and time, what we call 'justice' is often a product of established custom rather than immutable natural right; be wary of appeals to abstract first principles that ignore custom's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Might often determines what is regarded as just
rubrics_metrics.description: Unable to make what is just strong, men have made what is strong just. Justice without might is helpless; might without justice is tyrannical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the practical fact that power and authority shape perceptions of justice; political and social realities often convert strength into the appearance of justice unless balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority and established laws function as universal rules in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The only universal rules are the laws of the country in ordinary affairs, and of the majority in others — this arises from might rather than pure reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We follow the majority because they have more power; ancient laws have authority because they remove the root of difference by their uniqueness and endurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outward show signals power (spruce appearance as index of status)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be spruce is not altogether foolish, for it proves that a great number of people work for one; outward show (brocade, lackeys) produces respect because habit links person and paraphernalia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appearances and ceremonial trappings create social effects of respect and obedience by habit; do not underrate the social function of external signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference requires inconvenience
rubrics_metrics.description: Deference means 'Put yourself to inconvenience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although apparently silly, deference is socially correct because it signals willingness to subordinate oneself and thus sustains social bonds and hierarchies.
